articles.title_orig: U.S. pressed China on farm goods purchases, lifting soybean futures
articles.title_zh: U.S. pressed China on farm goods purchases, lifting soybean futures
articles.content_orig:
Soybean futures gave up earlier gains on Monday as traders looked ahead to a USDA crop report due this week
Scott Olson / Getty Images
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer pressed China to carry out its past commitments , including agricultural purchases, during a videoconference with Vice Premier He Lifeng. Soybean futures jumped by the most in more than two weeks following the U.S. appeal, according to Bloomberg , before giving up those gains.
Bessent raised concerns about recent Chinese actions and said Beijing must follow through on the pledges it made at the Busan meeting, the Treasury Department said. He said further advances hinge on tangible outcomes and that Washington will evaluate how China carries out the deal.
Greer said China must deliver tangible steps on buying farm goods, on rare earths and on other critical minerals, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. The office said the administration will monitor compliance with past commitments while pursuing balanced trade with China.
Traders balanced fresh optimism about Chinese buying against forecasts that the U.S. Department of Agriculture will show soybean output edging nearer to an all-time high, according to Bloomberg. Futures have fallen for four straight weeks.
China voiced "serious concerns" over the latest U.S. restrictions on trade and the economy during the call, according to Bloomberg. The two sides engaged in "frank, in-depth, and constructive exchanges" and agreed to deepen cooperation while keeping disagreements in check, Bloomberg said, citing a Chinese state news agency account of the call.
Chinese state-owned companies had reserved at least 20 shiploads of U.S. soybeans in mid-October , roughly 1.3 million tons, their first purchases since the late-September summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Beijing has committed to import at least 25 million tons of U.S. soybeans a year through 2028, along with $17 billion a year in other U.S. farm goods.
In September, Bessent said some Chinese deliverables had fallen short and that China was running late on some of its agricultural commitments, according to Bloomberg. The two governments agreed to push their trade truce out to Jan. 10.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo delivers veiled rebuke of austerity measures in predecessor’s homeland
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo delivers veiled rebuke of austerity measures in predecessor’s homeland
articles.content_orig:
Pontiff tells Argentina’s president the economy must benefit all on second stop of 12-day Latin America tour
Pope Leo XIV has delivered a stinging critique of Argentine president Javier Milei’s harsh austerity measures, insisting growth must benefit all in a speech met with rapturous applause in Buenos Aires.
“The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy,” he said on Sunday, shortly after landing in Argentina on the second leg of a Latin America tour.
Leo stressed the plight of those who, “despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household’s needs”.
He spoke out in defence of the poor and pensioners, insisting that “particular concern be shown for those affected by illness, dependency and disability” – a veiled reference to the government’s controversial cuts to disability assistance.
He also told Milei, known for his foul-mouthed diatribes, that strengthening democracy required a “willingness to listen” and the “careful use of words”.
Leo, 71, is on an ambitious 12-day tour of the continent, just three weeks after undergoing surgery for lung cancer .
The visit is the first by a pontiff to Argentina in nearly four decades, and Leo was met with calls to help mend deep divisions in the country after three years of austerity under Milei.
Argentina is the home country of the late pope, Francis, who Milei famously insulted for his pro-poor teachings.
Leo said he was “retracing” Francis’s steps.
Argentines are hoping the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics will help unite the country, which is bitterly divided between supporters and opponents of Milei.
“Just like the World Cup unites us, hopefully the pope will too,” said Liliana Deblauwe, a 68-year-old retired teacher who waited with hundreds of people to see the pope visit a monument to liberation hero Jose de San Martin.
Hundreds more chanting “Papa Leon” (Spanish for Leo) gathered outside the presidential palace, where he was hosted by Milei.
Brian Inacio Rodriguez, a 26-year-old job seeker, spent five days travelling overland from Ushuaia, at the very tip of South America, to see the pontiff.
He said he hoped he brought “much peace to Argentina”.
Leo arrived in Buenos Aires from Uruguay, where he began his first trip as pope to Latin America, the world’s most Catholic continent which is becoming increasingly secular.
In Uruguay, he condemned drug violence and urged an end to child poverty.
In Buenos Aires, he insisted on the importance of “personal integrity” in public office, stressing that “corruption undermines the confidence of citizens in their institutions.”
The Argentine stage of his visit aims to boost the flagging faith of a country left disappointed by Francis’s failure to visit during his papacy.
It will also act as a litmus test of support for the church. In a recent University of Buenos Aires poll, 57.7% of people identified as Catholic, down from about 90% in the 1960s.
Leo will visit a home for disabled people and a prison and celebrate three open-air masses.
The church has said it expects 7 million to attend the various events.
Milei came to office on a promise to revive Argentina’s ailing economy and tame runaway inflation by shrinking the welfare state, targeting public hospitals, universities and pensioners in particular.
The poverty rate has swung wildly since he came to power – increasing to 32.3% in September.
A close ally of US president Donald Trump, with a similar combative style, Milei had a tense relationship with Francis.
On the campaign trail the cost-cutting economist called his countryman an “imbecile” for championing social justice.
Once in office, however, he softened his tone, but he continues to heap insults on the press and opposition.
His relationship with Leo has so far been cordial, but the local Catholic church has heavily criticised him for treating key social services solely as a budgetary constraint.
Milei has also been criticised for restricting several democratic freedoms, including the right to protest. But he maintains a loyal supporter base for drastically reducing inflation.

Minister delivered a letter to Taipei’s representatives urging name change before October 1, Lithuanian news portal reports
The government of Lithuania asked Taipei to change the name of a controversial representative office in Vilnius before Beijing’s National Day last month, according to explosive media reports in the tiny Baltic state.
Reports in Delfi, a Lithuanian news portal, on Monday said a deputy foreign minister delivered a letter to Taipei’s representatives – including the head of the “Taiwanese Representative Office” – on September 24, asking them to change the office’s name by October 1.

articles.title_orig: US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
articles.title_zh: US-led peace talks for Russia and Ukraine will look at security guarantees for both sides
articles.content_orig:
Officials from Ukraine, Russia and the United States are set to converge in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for negotiations aimed at ending nearly five years of war between Moscow and Kyiv.
But analysts are not hopeful of much progress in the trilateral talks slated for Tuesday and Wednesday amid US President Donald Trump’s recent engagement with the Kremlin.
Trump has blamed President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for holding up peace efforts. “Zelenskyy has to want to settle this war, and if he doesn’t, I think it’s going to be a very bad thing,” he said last month. The US also signed a deal last month to buy Russian diesel, which critics say would provide Russia with revenue to sustain the war against Ukraine.
On Thursday, Trump claimed that the war was close to being settled , and ending it might involve all of Europe. But Europe is not officially part of the trilateral talks. Last week, France said that Europe will send representatives to Abu Dhabi, as Ukraine’s Western allies fear Trump might force a deal that might undermine the continent’s security.
Russia occupies roughly 20 percent of Ukraine, including Crimea and parts of the eastern Donbas region. The Russian move has not been recognised by the international community, but Trump has urged Kyiv to cede territory for a deal to end the war that has killed thousands and displaced millions.
So what can we expect from the latest round of peace talks this year, as tit-for-tat attacks on energy sites have intensified in recent months? The two sides have held three rounds of US-mediated peace talks this year, including two in Abu Dhabi.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will be heading the US delegation for the first such talks in nine months, as the US president has pushed to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
Ukraine’s primary negotiator and foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov will lead Kyiv’s negotiation team, the Kyiv Independent reported. The Ukrainian delegation will also include David Arakhamia, head of Zelenskyy’s parliamentary group; Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov; and Sergiy Kyslytsya, first deputy head of the Presidential Office.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, confirmed last week that the Russian delegation would be led by former Culture Minister Vladimir Medinsky, the state news agency TASS reported. It also includes diplomat Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yuri Zhygarlovsky, the Kremlin said.
On Monday, the Kremlin said the peace talks would not include European officials. Peskov’s comments to reporters appeared to conflict with a statement on Sunday by French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot, who said officials from France, Britain, Germany, NATO and the European Commission would be present at the November 10-11 meeting.
An EU official told the AFP news agency on Monday that national security officials for the bloc, NATO, France, Germany and the United Kingdom would be on site – but it was unclear how they would be involved.
“I don’t expect any tangible progress in the Abu Dhabi talks. The reason is simple and remains the same – Putin has absolutely no intention to negotiate seriously. He remains totally fixated on the [destruction] of Ukraine,” Oleksandr Merezhko, a Ukrainian member of parliament from the Servant of the People party, told Al Jazeera.
Putin wants Ukraine’s “surrender”, which will allow him to subjugate Ukrainians, he said.
Finnish-Russian political scientist Arkady Moshes says Ukraine’s sovereignty and independence are at stake in the upcoming talks.
Restoring Ukrainian territorial integrity, including Crimea, may already be beyond reach, said Moshes, a programme director at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. Russia annexed the Crimean peninsula in 2014 – a move not recognised by the United Nations.
Moshes said that it would be very difficult for Ukraine to accept a peace agreement that doesn’t allow it “to choose its alliances, decide on its security future, or [that] put limits on its military”.
Ukraine wants Russia to withdraw from its territory and a security guarantee as part of any deal with Russia, but Russia has refused to end its occupation and set conditions that Kyiv should not be given membership of the NATO alliance. Moscow has also opposed the deployment of foreign troops in Ukraine after a deal.
Matthew Boyse, a senior fellow with Hudson Institute’s Center on Europe and Eurasia specialising in Central Europe, agreed that the most difficult sticking points are those about territory and security guarantees for Ukraine.
“So far Putin has not budged from his ‘my way or the highway’ and ‘what’s mine is mine and what’s yours is negotiable’ position,” Boyse, a former US diplomat, told Al Jazeera.
The analysts agreed that the future of European security as a whole is also at stake.
“The Kremlin agreed to and codified the post-1991 European security order in many agreements and treaties until Putin in the 2000s began to tear them up and in 2014 turned that order upside down,” said Boyse, referring to Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014.
But the Kremlin has accused the US and its European allies of encircling Russia militarily. To that end, Russia has opposed the expansion of NATO in Europe, which it sees as a security threat. Russia has warned of a direct military standoff with Europe if NATO expands its military footprint eastward closer to the Russian border.
Anders Olofsgard, deputy director at the Stockholm Institute of Transition Economics, said it was reassuring that Kushner had explicitly stated that “NATO would remain central to European collective defence and that no country should have a veto over another country’s security or alliance choices”.
Another element at stake is the future of post-Soviet states in Europe, namely Belarus, Moldova, Georgia and Armenia, said Moshes, the political scientist.
“If Ukraine now capitulates despite its serious efforts and despite the support from the West, from Europe, that means that several other post-Soviet states will definitely be under threat,” he said, adding that Russia could pursue a “tough Soviet-like sphere of influence or even direct annexation” of these countries.
No talks have yet come close to a breakthrough.
Only perhaps at the end of March 2022, at the very start of the conflict, when the two countries met in Istanbul, there was some possibility of ending the conflict, said Olofsgard.
“At this point, the relative strengths of the two counterparts were not clear; Ukraine had proven stronger and Russia more incompetent than expected,” he said.
Ukraine was also more willing to make concessions with respect to joining NATO, not allowing foreign bases in Ukraine, and not demanding the immediate return of Crimea, Olofsgard added.
Ultimately, however, there were many factors contributing to the meeting’s failure in the end, “including the atrocities in Bucha, [a] lack of clear Western promises of security guarantees, Russian failures on the battlefield changing the calculations of both sides, and incompatible views on land concessions and military build-up of Ukraine”, he said.
Analysts talk about a guarantor to secure peace. They point out the example of American troops stationed in South Korea to this day following the 1953 Korean War armistice.
Ukraine would “probably need something like that”, Moshes said, adding that “no Western country has been seriously speaking about guaranteeing whatever the outcome of the negotiations might be”.
Vast differences remain between the two sides.
While past meetings have facilitated important results, from prisoner exchanges to the return of kidnapped Ukrainian children from Russia, they have failed to address core differences, said Boyse, referring to territorial concessions and a security guarantee for Ukraine.
Ultimately, Russia wants to win the war – it wants a military victory over a diplomatic one, said Moshes.

articles.title_orig: Google’s chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia’s own AI boom
articles.title_zh: Google’s chip business is on a faster track than Nvidia’s own AI boom
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia ( NVDA ) is investigating its own CEO. Google is busy building the chips that could take its customers.
Nvidia quickly sunk 8% after the opening bell Monday, trading at its lowest level since March, as its board looks into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy . Alphabet ( GOOGL ) is up about 3%. It's the latest chapter in Wall Street's first $4.5 trillion CEO scandal .
Google introduced two new tensor processing units, or TPUs — its homegrown AI chips — on Monday. The TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max join the 8t and 8i it unveiled in April, the first time Google has introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Both new chips ship next year.
Think of it as a chip menu. The 8tx keeps data encrypted for governments, banks, and other regulated businesses, paired with processors from AMD ( AMD ). The 8i Max squeezes two chips into one package for requests with long context windows — the amount of information an AI model can juggle at once.
The forecasts are the eye-popper. Bloomberg Intelligence sees TPU sales rising from about $12 billion this year to more than $135 billion by 2028, not counting chips rented through Google Cloud. That's more than 11-fold in two years.
Nvidia's data center business grew nearly eightfold in the first two years of the AI boom, from $15 billion in fiscal 2023 to $115 billion in fiscal 2025.
The chips are already flying off the line. Epoch AI estimates TPU shipments doubled in computing power in a single quarter this year, to roughly 800,000 chips.
Anthropic is the headliner. Its IPO filing shows about $161 billion of lease payments tied to TPUs, which Raymond James says makes it the biggest custom-chip customer of Google's design partner, Broadcom ( AVGO ). Meta ( META ), OpenAI and Oracle ( ORCL ) are buyers too.
Google used to roll out about one data center TPU a year. Now it has one for every job.
Nvidia still has the bigger engine.
Its next-generation Rubin chip is rated at 35 petaflops — a measure of raw computing speed — compared with about 10 for Google's 8i and about 20 for the 8i Max, according to Yahoo Finance calculations.
Google is selling on price. SemiAnalysis found that Google's current Ironwood TPU delivers up to nearly three times as much AI output per dollar as Nvidia's Blackwell chips when running AI agents, though Nvidia's top system still wins when speed is everything.
Forecasts aren't sales, and Nvidia still sells far more AI chips than anyone else.
Nvidia's next big moment comes Nov. 17, when it reports third quarter results, a day before a requested closed-door House briefing on CEO Jensen Huang . Investors will want to hear whether customers are hedging their bets. As Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon wrote to clients, "Jensen is not an ordinary CEO; he IS NVIDIA."

articles.title_orig: Alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia chief pitched AI chips deals to investors
articles.title_zh: Alleged Chinese spy linked to Nvidia chief pitched AI chips deals to investors
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia stock fell more than 6% on Monday after the tech giant launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.
U.S. intelligence agencies said Alice Huang, an executive at cloud company MegaSpeed, has been passing information to Beijing, according to reports in The New York Times and The Financial Times.
Nvidia said its board has launched an independent investigation following the reports that Huang was the target of a "foreign intelligence effort."
Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it," the company said in a Sunday statement .
The co-founder and CEO told staff in an email that he had "fallen short" of his responsibility to serve his colleagues, the board, partners and shareholders around the world.
"I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," Huang said in the email.
China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday the "so-called Chinese spy narrative" was unsubstantiated, Reuters reported.
The probe has sparked questions about Huang's future as CEO of the company.
But any talk of replacing Huang is "comedy," Dan Ives, senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe."
While the probe and affair is a "game changer" for the CEO and company, it doesn't alter the view that Nvidia remains two to three years ahead of China in AI chips, Ives said.
"You're talking about what I would view as a torchbearer — the leader of AI technology — not just in the U.S. but globally. So I think the fact that we're in this situation, from an investor perspective, the clear worry is, does Jensen stay on as CEO? The Street would say probably likely, but given the board investigation, anything could happen, and that creates a huge uncertainty."
Tech stocks took a hammering last week as investors reassessed the data center build-out after Democrats won control of Congress.
Asian tech stocks rose across the region on Monday, rebounding from Friday's losses. Shares of U.S. chipmakers also climbed, with AMD , Marvell , Arm , Intel and Qualcomm rising on Monday.
Joachim Klement, investment strategist at Panmure Liberum, said the impact is currently contained to Nvidia.
But if Huang's position is "endangered," then "Nvidia might cut back on supporting other companies, whether it's in Asia or in the U.S., that might then spread a little bit more into the other semiconductor names," he said.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday praised Huang's leadership but said he hadn't spoken to the CEO about the investigation.
"I think he's an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it," the president told reporters.
"He's done an amazing job for our country," Trump added.
Shaun Maguire, partner at Sequoia, also defended the tech giant CEO, saying in a post on X that Huang is "one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation."
He added: "two mistakes don't make a right, and I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America's AI leadership."
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk reshared Maguire's post, adding that he agrees with the venture capitalist's statements.
Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and will hold a major conference in Washington, D.C., at the end of the month.
— CNBC's Kif Leswing and Kamaron McNair helped contribute to this report.

articles.title_orig: Sanctioned Russian military aircraft lands at Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel
articles.title_zh: Sanctioned Russian military aircraft lands at Ben-Gurion Airport in Israel
articles.content_orig:
A jet operated by the Russian Defense Ministry landed in Israel's Ben-Gurion Airport on Sunday evening, flight-tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed.
The Tupolev Tu-154M, which departed from a military base near Moscow , has been on the US sanctions list since 2023.
The Chkalovsky Air Base from which the flight originated is the primary operational hub for the Russian Defense Ministry, which manages VIP transport and government missions for high-ranking military officials and official delegations.
The flight path went over the Black Sea and through Turkish airspace before entering Israel from the Mediterranean. The plane circled over Israel before landing at Ben-Gurion Airport at about 7 p.m.
Flightradar24 data showed that in the past week, the aircraft has remained in Moscow since arriving from Novosibirsk on November 2.
The aircraft belongs to the 223rd Flight Unit of the Russian Defense Ministry, itself a sanctioned entity, as the US State Department accused the unit of transporting personnel and equipment belonging to the Wagner mercenary group to countries where Wagner operated.
The aircraft was listed under Executive Order 14024, which authorizes sanctions targeting Russia's harmful foreign activities, including those connected to its war against Ukraine.
As part of the May 19, 2023, action, the US identified 37 aircraft associated with the unit as blocked property, including RA-85042.
When approached by The Jerusalem Post , the Russian Embassy in Israel declined to comment on who was in the aircraft or why they were in Israel.
Additionally, the IDF declined the Post's request for comment.
The Post also reached out to several US government bodies for comment.

articles.title_orig: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Israeli opposition eyes deal with ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to oust Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Avigdor Liberman's 2018 haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription proposal has reemerged as a potential basis for coalition negotiations after the Yisrael Beytenu chairman signaled on Sunday that he was willing to compromise with ultra-Orthodox parties. But how does the proposal compare with the draft legislation promoted by Boaz Bismuth in 2025, and would either framework meet the IDF's growing manpower needs?
The 2018 proposal, developed by the Defense Ministry and the IDF during Liberman's tenure as defense minister, sought to gradually increase haredi enlistment while preserving military service deferrals for yeshiva students. It established annual recruitment targets, financial penalties for institutions that failed to meet them, and a mechanism that could ultimately terminate the special exemption arrangement if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
Unlike Bismuth's proposal, which introduced additional personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students, Liberman's framework primarily targeted yeshiva funding and the continued validity of the exemption system itself. It also set a lower exemption age of 24, compared with 26 under Bismuth's proposal.
The differences have taken on renewed political significance as Gadi Eisenkot prepares to receive the mandate to form a government. Liberman's decision to lift his veto on cooperation with haredi parties has opened the door to coalition negotiations, although he maintains that his willingness to compromise does not amount to abandoning his support for universal conscription.
"Willingness to compromise does not mean abandoning values and principles," Liberman wrote in a statement on Sunday, defending his change in political position amid criticism from commentators and journalists.
He emphasized that his 2018 proposal would require adjustments in light of the October 7 attacks and the subsequent increase in the military's manpower requirements.
"It is clear to me that following the events of October 7, the law I proposed in 2018 also requires changes and adjustments, but it still constitutes a suitable basis for reaching agreements," he wrote.
Liberman's 2018 legislation was developed by a committee comprising representatives of the Defense Ministry and the IDF. It passed its first reading in the Knesset in July of that year.
The proposal aimed to increase military enlistment among ultra-Orthodox men without dismantling the existing yeshiva system. It allowed many students to continue deferring their service while establishing gradually increasing recruitment targets.
Bismuth's 2025 proposal similarly preserved the possibility of service deferrals and exemptions but added personal restrictions intended to encourage enlistment.
Neither proposal established an immediate and equal military conscription requirement for all young haredi men.
One of the most significant differences between the proposals concerned the age at which yeshiva students could receive exemptions from military service. Liberman's framework set the exemption age at 24, while Bismuth's proposed legislation raised it to 26.
The enforcement mechanisms also differed substantially.
Under Liberman's framework, annual recruitment targets were accompanied by financial sanctions against yeshivas if those targets were not met.
The proposal's most consequential provision addressed prolonged failures to meet recruitment quotas. If actual enlistment remained below 85% of the annual target for three consecutive years, the amendment to the law would expire after an additional 12 months.
This meant that the special arrangement allowing military service deferrals and exemptions could not continue indefinitely if recruitment targets were repeatedly missed.
However, Liberman's proposal did not establish a new system of personal sanctions against individual yeshiva students who failed to enlist.
Instead, its enforcement mechanisms focused primarily on financial penalties for religious institutions and the continued validity of the exemption system.
The committee that developed the framework also recommended expanding administrative sanctions against deserters and draft evaders.
Bismuth's proposal, by contrast, introduced personal sanctions alongside financial penalties for yeshivas that failed to comply with the law.
Those proposed restrictions included limitations on overseas travel, obtaining a new driver's license before age 23, and eligibility for certain government benefits and economic incentives.
However, the personal sanctions were not all designed to take effect automatically or immediately.
Some depended on the issuance of an enlistment order and the individual's subsequent failure to report for duty. Others were linked to failures to meet broader recruitment targets, while certain restrictions were subject to age limits or delayed implementation dates.
The proposal also included provisions allowing sanctions to be eased or exemptions to be granted under specified circumstances.
For individual yeshiva students, Bismuth's framework was therefore more stringent because it introduced additional personal restrictions.
On the exemption system as a whole, however, Liberman's proposal established a potentially more far-reaching consequence for persistent failures to meet recruitment targets.
Under his framework, the special legislative arrangement could expire following three consecutive years of missed targets, subject to the stipulated 12-month transition period.
Bismuth's proposal included review mechanisms, financial sanctions, and possible adjustments, but did not establish an equivalent automatic mechanism terminating the entire exemption arrangement.
The differences are also evident in the recruitment targets themselves.
Liberman's framework established a target of 3,996 recruits in 2018, gradually increasing to 4,967 in 2021 and 6,208 in 2025.
One version of Bismuth's framework set a target of 8,160 recruits over 18 months, averaging about 5,440 per year.
Under that version, up to 10% of the recruitment target could be met by individuals performing civilian service in security-related fields.
At first glance, Bismuth's initial target appears higher than the target Liberman established for 2018. However, Bismuth's annual average was lower than the target Liberman's proposal established for 2025.
The figures do not represent identical periods or legislative arrangements operating under equivalent timetables.
Several versions of the recruitment targets were presented during the advancement of Bismuth's framework. Each figure must therefore be examined in light of the specific legislative version and period it refers to.
Another significant difference concerns how recruits are counted.
Liberman's framework established targets for national and civilian service separately from military enlistment targets.
Under one version of Bismuth's proposal, civilian service in security-related fields could count toward the overall recruitment quota, up to 10% of the target.
Consequently, meeting the overall quota would not necessarily indicate that an equivalent number of new soldiers had joined the IDF.
The identity of those included in the recruitment figures has also sparked controversy.
One criticism of Bismuth's framework concerned the possibility of counting young men who had already left the haredi community.
If a young man raised in the ultra-Orthodox community but no longer studying at a yeshiva is counted as a haredi recruit, meeting the recruitment target does not necessarily demonstrate increased enlistment among students attending active yeshivas.
Beyond these legal and numerical differences lies a fundamental change in Israel's security requirements.
Liberman's proposal was developed in 2018, five years before the October 7 attacks and the war that followed.
Since then, the haredi population has grown, while the IDF's manpower requirements have increased significantly.

articles.title_orig: How a bank collapse left millions in limbo and toppled Paraguay's president
articles.title_zh: How a bank collapse left millions in limbo and toppled Paraguay's president
articles.content_orig:
Protesters hold signs outside Congress in Asunción, Paraguay, on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. The Senate impeached and removed President Santiago Peña over allegations linked to the collapse of Ueno Bank. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as his successor. Jorge Saenz/AP hide caption
ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — When Ueno Bank's services abruptly stopped working in the early hours of Tuesday morning , the consequences were immediate for the millions of Paraguayans who had come to depend on it for everyday transactions.
"People don't have any trust," said Elizabeth González, a 28-year-old barista at a café in downtown Asunción, a few blocks from Paraguay's Congress building, where protesters had begun gathering after the bank's collapse was announced Tuesday.
Earlier, one customer had walked into the café and insisted on paying in cash. He no longer trusted any bank.
"If Paraguayans themselves aren't confident right now, foreign investors will be less so," González said.
The collapse affected far more than the bank's shareholders. Ueno said it had 2.9 million customers — around 60% of Paraguay's adult population. The Central Bank said the bank had approximately 1.8 million depositors.
By Saturday, authorities said almost 1.2 million customers had received an advance payment under the state's deposit guarantee fund, but many were still waiting.
A shuttered Ueno Bank ATM in Asunción, Paraguay, after the bank's collapse left millions of customers unable to access their money and disrupted everyday transactions across the country. Charles Parkinson for NPR hide caption
It also led to the removal of President Santiago Peña, a close ally of President Donald Trump, and exposed a power struggle inside within the ruling Colorado Party.
The anger was palpable outside Congress on Friday, where hundreds had gathered to protest not only their inability to access their money but also what they saw as a broader failure of accountability.
"I came not because it affects me personally, but because it affects all of Paraguay," said Elodia Saveredo, a 71-year-old housewife who sells her own handicrafts online.
Betarram Caballero, a 23-year-old fifth-year biochemistry student and president of the student center at the National University of Asunción, said classmates had money frozen that they needed to cover basic expenses.
"It wasn't a lot of money, perhaps, but it was money for their bus fare. It was money for their food," she said. "To hear that and not be able to do anything because I don't have the resources to help them is very discouraging."
Ueno Bank launched as a fintech in 2021 and began operating as a bank in November 2023. Its meteoric rise to become one of Paraguay's most prominent financial institutions was driven in part by slick marketing and a digital model built around convenience and cashback deals. Customers could open accounts on their phones and access incentives through merchant partnerships and promotional offers.
Caballero believes the crisis was foretold by an intense campaign in the days before accounts were frozen.
"They were bombarding us with messages telling us to put our money there," she said. "There were also rumors about what was already on the cards."
Demonstrators burn a flag depicting the Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest over the banking crisis outside the National Congress in Asunción on Nov. 6, 2026. Jose Bogado/AFP hide caption
The bank also held substantial public funds. Paraguay's Social Security Institute (IPS) had approximately $355 million invested in Ueno, equivalent to around 9% of its total investment portfolio.
The sums involved have raised questions about how such a young bank came to hold so much public money.
Manuel Ferreira, an economist and former finance minister, told local outlet ABC Color that the collapse raised fundamental questions about how the bank managed its assets. He pointed out that, in a typical bank, shareholders provide only a small portion of the money behind its assets, while the bulk comes from customer deposits.
He also argued that marketing and discounts helped attract customers but did not create lasting assets. A bank's principal asset, he said, was its loan portfolio:  money owed by borrowers.
But in the case of Ueno, many of those loans had gone to companies directly linked to the bank's controlling owners, Grupo Vásquez, including $146 million in loans made to just three companies. Ferreira described Ueno's promissory notes as being signed by the same people on both sides of some transactions.
The scandal hit Peña particularly hard because of his personal links to the bank's holding company, in which he held shares even after taking up the presidency. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, who had led Ueno Bank, to head Paraguay's Central Bank in 2023.
In his asset declaration submitted weeks after taking up the presidency in 2023, Peña listed shares in Ueno Holding, then valued at around $845,000. Those shares represented around 1.6% of the company's paid-up capital when he later sold them in March 2025.
Paraguayan President Santiago Peña signs his resignation letter at the presidential residence in Asunción on Nov. 5, 2026, days after the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank amid a solvency crisis that left millions of customers unable to access their savings. Laura Fioravanti/AP hide caption
Prosecutors allege that, while president, he used his position to influence public agencies and state-owned entities to maintain deposits with the bank despite his connections to its parent group.
Peña resigned Thursday and was removed from office Friday. The following day, prosecutors charged him with breach of trust and administration for personal gain. He was ordered held in pretrial detention at a military facility pending the investigation. Peña has pleaded not guilty. Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, has been sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028.
Carvallo was also arrested and charged with breach of trust, administration for personal gain and producing false public documents. A judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a police facility. Eight Ueno executives, including 36-year-old CEO Miguel Vásquez, were also arrested and charged.
The crisis has also put the spotlight on Horacio Cartes, a tobacco magnate and former president of Paraguay who wields considerable political and economic influence.
Cartes handpicked Peña, his former finance minister, to lead his Honor Colorado faction into the 2023 presidential election. But the relationship between the two men had become increasingly strained, apparently over Peña's efforts to establish his own power base within the party.
In September, senators aligned with Cartes sought information from the Central Bank about Ueno's transactions with related companies and its public-sector deposits.
After the bank collapsed, Cartes publicly distanced himself from Peña, releasing a public statement on Wednesday calling for an investigation and insisting there should be "no impunity for anyone." The following day, his faction backed Peña's removal.
The move was widely seen as a decisive withdrawal of political protection for Peña, and an opportunity for Cartes to reassert his influence.
Demonstrators burn Ueno Bank cards during a protest after Paraguay's central bank took over the bank amid a solvency crisis in Asunción, Paraguay, Nov. 5, 2026. Jorge Saenz/AP hide caption
But for those gathered outside Congress protesting, the scandal was about more than a bank collapse. It was a reckoning with Paraguay's political establishment.
For Rodrigo Piatti, a 45-year-old activist with the anti-corruption campaign group Comisión Escrache Ciudadano, the scandal would only lead to real change if the political establishment, including Cartes, were challenged.
"Everything that's wrong with Paraguay… is Horacio Cartes and his line of succession," Piatti said. "[Paraguay needs] the opposition to take power. A real o

articles.content_orig:
Speakers at International Forum on Mutual Learning among Civilisations explore how China’s policies could set global example
China’s global policies could offer an alternative to Western approaches to tackling international challenges, speakers at a forum in Macau have said, noting that the nation’s development and achievements are most acutely felt in that city and in Hong Kong.
At the second edition of the International Forum on Mutual Learning among Civilisations, which opened on Monday in Macau, speakers also said that lessons from history could inspire new approaches to modern problems.
“China’s global policy is quite opposite to what we have today in the world order in the West. There is, I would say, some inclination towards unipolarity,” Jasna Plevnik, president of the Croatian think tank, Geoeconomic Forum Croatia, told the South China Morning Post.

articles.title_orig: Rochefort's Kyle Bass on Nvidia probe, China: President Trump is in a 'difficult spot'
articles.title_zh: Rochefort's Kyle Bass on Nvidia probe, China: President Trump is in a 'difficult spot'
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he was ordering the Justice Department to investigate Democratic leaders over what he described as threats against Republican officials, donors and supporters, without identifying the alleged communications or providing evidence of criminal conduct.
"The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States, and others, with Impeachment and many other forms of punishment, even though they admit they have no reason to do so," Trump said in a Truth Social post .
The alleged threats, the president said, are "extortion at the highest level," he wrote. "I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!"
In his post, Trump claimed that Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan is planning to "go after all young people that believe in Republican Values."
Trump was apparently referencing a speech Slotkin made at a University of Chicago event on Oct. 13. At the time, Slotkin said: "I want young people coming out of school to say, 'Should I go work for the Trump administration?'...I want them to be like, 'Lord, that might be buying myself a ton of problems that I don't want. And so let me avoid participating in that.' I want that deterrence message sent."
Slotkin alleges that she, her family and her staff faced physical and legal intimidation after the posting of a November 2025 video in which Slotkin and other Democratic leaders called on the U.S. military to "refuse illegal orders" following the airstrikes targeting boats in the Caribbean.
On Nov. 20, Trump called the video treason and said "an example must be set."
The FBI contacted lawmakers, including Slotkin, days later. In February, Slotkin declined to sit for an interview the Justice Department requested about the video.
"The intimidation is the point, and I'm not gonna go along with that," the senator said in February. A federal grand jury later declined to indict the video participants.
Now, Trump alleges Democrats are threatening legal intimidation against Republican leaders and their supporters.
"Republicans should get smart, fast! Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders," the president wrote.
The White House and Slotkin didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Stock Slides After Huang Apologizes for Affair With Alleged Spy
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Nvidia Stock Slides After Huang Apologizes for Affair With Alleged Spy
articles.content_orig:
CEO reportedly ‌had close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing
Nvidia said ⁠on Sunday it “is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”.
The New York Times reported in ​October that Donald Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence that Huang ‌had a close relationship ‌with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to ‌Beijing.
Speaking to reporters on Sunday, Trump downplayed the revelations about Huang, who is an influential adviser to the president on artificial intelligence, saying: “I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it.”
Trump also brushed off a question about whether he now regrets not acting on the intelligence when he was briefed on it, and suggested that he would be happy to take Huang with him on a trip to Asia next week. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Trump said. “He dealt with somebody. But, you know, so does everybody else.”
Republican lawmakers have expressed more alarm, asking Huang to give the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees a closed-door briefing next week on Nvidia’s “security protocols against foreign adversary espionage” and his relationship with Alice Huang or Huang Le, an executive at a Singapore-based datacenter company called Megaspeed, who is of no relation to the Nvidia CEO. She had previously been suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, prompting American officials to surveil and monitor her.
Those officials have determined that she was acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times reported, citing unnamed sources.
The company’s board said in a statement on Sunday that, while it has no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry will examine all available information.
“The Board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders,” the company said. “The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate.”
Huang fully ‌supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it, it added.
Axios reported on ​Sunday, citing a draft email by Huang to employees, that Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and took full ⁠responsibility for his actions.
“I was unfaithful to my ​wife. My ​actions hurt her ​and our children. There is no excuse ​for what ‌I did,” ​Huang said ​in the draft email also seen by Reuters.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Axios report.
The Times reported on Sunday that a memo drafted by US secretary of state Marco Rubio circulated among top policymakers in the Trump administration last spring, citing intelligence that the businesswoman who had a relationship with Nvidia’s chief executive was a spy for China’s ministry of state security. Despite those concerns, Huang was invited to join Trump’s delegation when he traveled to China in May. Huang and his wife, Lori Huang, were also invited to a state dinner at the White House in September for Xi Jinping and seated at the top table with Trump and China’s president.
Nvidia’s powerful chips serve as a cornerstone of the AI boom, placing Jensen Huang into one of the most influential leadership positions in the industry. In that position, he has developed a close partnership with Trump as the US government attempts to defend its position as a leader in AI development.
However, national security concerns have prompted strict US export controls, effectively barring the company from selling its top-tier processors to customers in China.
US officials have cited threats to the US supply chain and fears over national security risks as a rationale for the restrictions. Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, has also suggested that China could be sanctioned for theft of US data and intellectual property.
The Trump administration has imposed restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China as a matter of national security. Megaspeed’s Alice Huang was suspected to have been helping the government get around those restrictions.
The investigation also follows a rough few days on Wall Street for AI tech firms, particularly Nvidia. A sell-off of tech stocks that began earlier this month and gained steam with disappointing earnings led to a total decline of nearly $1tn in value off the tech-heavy Nasdaq exchange in one week and erased about $2tn in a month.
A drop of 3.1% for Nvidia, previously worth about $5tn, whose chips have made it the poster child of the AI frenzy, was the heaviest force pulling the S&P 500 downward recently.
Nick Robins-Early and Blake Montgomery contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: ‘Forever cruise’ ship Odyssey impounded in Singapore, records show
articles.title_zh: ‘Forever cruise’ ship Odyssey impounded in Singapore, records show
articles.content_orig:
The Odyssey, the "forever cruise" that has been stranded in Southeast Asia after its owner struggled with financial problems , has been arrested in Singapore, according to court records obtained by CBS News.
A Singaporean law firm, Helmsman LLC, is listed as the arresting solicitor, but it is unclear whom the firm is representing. A source familiar with the matter tells CBS News that it is likely a fuel supplier.
The luxury cruise ship is currently being operated by its lender after its owner, Villa Vie Residences, couldn't keep up with payments.
Villa Vie owes one supplier in the area approximately $500,000, though it's unclear whether that supplier hired the law firm to solicit the arrest.
A ship arrest is a legal process in which a vessel can be detained or seized following a legal claim.
The journey of the MV Odyssey luxury cruise ship, launched in October 2024, came to a sudden end last month in Cambodia, where residents on the ship had just hours to disembark.
According to accounts from multiple sources familiar with the final weeks on board, these details included a scramble to find fuel while stuck at a port in Singapore, a rush by the crew to obtain provisions once food shipments had ended, and the temporary detainment of the ship in Hong Kong.
This story published first on CBS News at 6:24 p.m. on Nov. 8, 2026.

articles.title_orig: Goodyear CEO Mark Stewart Steps Down
articles.title_zh: Goodyear CEO Mark Stewart Steps Down
articles.content_orig:
Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co. announced Monday that CEO Mark Stewart would be stepping down from his role effective immediately.
Board member Roger Wood is taking over as interim CEO and president, Goodyear said.
The leadership change comes as the tire company is in the midst of a multiyear transformation plan .
Stewart was hired in January 2024 to lead the company, with the goal of revitalizing the legacy American business to make it more efficient and profitable.
The company has faced disappointing results thus far, reporting last week third-quarter results that saw net sales down 2.3% year over year and an adjusted net loss of $31 million. Goodyear failed to reach a 10% operating margin by the end of last year, which was a major goal of the turnaround plan.
Goodyear said it formed a special committee of the board earlier this year to conduct a "strategic review of the company's businesses and operations focused on identifying opportunities to strengthen performance and drive shareholder value."
It said Monday it will continue that work by evaluating strategic and operational initiatives that include further optimizing the company's business mix and footprint, improving efficiency and investing in new products and capabilities that support long-term growth.
"Goodyear has made meaningful progress in becoming a more efficient and focused company, and the board believes this is the right moment to transition leadership to accelerate that progress and capture additional opportunity," Goodyear Chair Joe Hinrichs said in a press release .
The company has faced headwinds from tariffs, higher raw material costs and increased competition from China .
Wood has been a member of the company's board of directors since July 2023 and was previously the co-CEO of Tenneco as well as CEO of Dana Holding Corporation.
The company will start a search for a permanent replacement as part of its strategic review.
Shares of Goodyear were down roughly 4% in early trading Monday.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | NYSE to Settle Tokenized Stocks on Avalanche Blockchain
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | NYSE to Settle Tokenized Stocks on Avalanche Blockchain
articles.content_orig:
More firms are joining us to support Issuer Sponsored Tokenized Securities on the new NYSE-affiliated venue for trading tokenized securities.
NYSE has already signed agreements with Securitize ( NYSE: SECZ ) and tZERO , and has now added agreements with four more firms:
The group includes both digital-native and established providers. Securitize, Superstate, and tZERO bring blockchain-native infrastructure, on-chain recordkeeping, and digital asset expertise. Computershare, Equiniti, and Broadridge bring decades of transfer agent experience, long-standing issuer relationships, and operational scale, and together, they serve close to 5,000 publicly listed companies, including nearly 99% of the S&P 500.
This announcement continues the NYSE’s long history of reimagining market infrastructure through thoughtful and deliberate innovation. Our priority remains protecting and upholding market integrity through every technological advancement, and we are thrilled to partner with like-minded organizations as we shape the future of finance.
Lynn Martin President, NYSE Group
The new digital platform will enable tokenized trading experiences, including 24/7 operations, instant settlement, orders sized in dollar amounts, and stablecoin-based funding. Its design combines the NYSE’s cutting-edge Pillar matching engine with blockchain-based post-trade systems, including the capability to support multiple chains for settlement and custody.
As a tokenization leader processing more than $360 billion in assets every day, we are excited to support the NYSE’s tokenization initiatives. Broadridge’s horizontal governance layer and integrated digital and traditional transfer agency services simplifies complexity for issuers irrespective of where their shares are tokenized and held.
The evolution of capital markets depends on combining innovation with the trust, resilience and investor protections that issuers and shareholders expect. As the first transfer agent to offer Issuer-Sponsored Tokens, we are pleased to be working with the NYSE on this initiative and believe ISTs have the potential to expand choice while maintaining the high standards of governance, transparency and shareholder servicing that underpin modern markets.
Ann Bowering CEO, Issuer Services, North America, Computershare
Tokenization has the potential to modernize how securities are issued, held and transferred, while preserving the protections and rights that issuers and shareholders rely on today. We’re proud to work with the NYSE to bring Equiniti’s transfer agent expertise, issuer relationships and operational scale to this next generation of market infrastructure.
Bringing capital markets onchain requires collaboration across the financial industry. We were proud to be selected as NYSE's first digital transfer agent and a premier design partner in developing the infrastructure for tokenized securities. Expanding the ecosystem is an important step toward making tokenized securities a core part of how capital markets operate. We look forward to continuing our work with NYSE to build the next generation of market infrastructure.
Carlos Domingo Chairman and CEO, Securitize
We’re proud to work with the New York Stock Exchange to modernize how securities trade, settle, and move. Tokenization is a partnership between issuers, transfer agents, and exchanges, and that future is happening today.
Robert Leshner CEO, Superstate
The NYSE’s approach to tokenized securities represents an important step toward bringing blockchain-based infrastructure into mainstream financial markets. As a pioneer in tokenization and regulated digital asset infrastructure, tZERO brings deep experience in supporting the issuance, ownership and transfer of tokenized securities – including the digital transfer agent regulated layer and proprietary technology. We look forward to working with the NYSE to help build the infrastructure that will enable issuers and investors to realize the benefits of tokenization at scale.
Pending regulatory approval, the platform will power a new NYSE-affiliated venue for trading tokenized securities. That includes both third-party custodial tokens and issuer sponsored tokenized securities. Both types are fungible with traditionally issued securities, so people who hold tokenized shares will get the same dividends and governance rights as other shareholders. The venue is built around established market structure principles, with distribution via non-discriminatory access to all participating broker-dealers.
For more than two centuries, the NYSE has reshaped how markets operate, and as part of ICE, which has been at the forefront of market innovation for more than 25 years, it continues to lead the industry in the development of on-chain infrastructure for trading, settlement, custody, and capital formation.

articles.title_orig: Why is there so much kissing in Spain?
articles.title_zh: Why is there so much kissing in Spain?
articles.content_orig:
In Spain, kissing in public is an everyday sight. But the country's comfort with public affection reveals a surprising history of repression and rebellion.
Kissing is everywhere in Spain. There's the double-cheek kiss when you meet someone, of course. But then there are the romantic ones. I've been stuck behind a middle-aged couple who stop to smooch on a busy high street. I've felt a pang of nostalgia seeing teens kissing in sun-soaked parks and I've squeezed past tipsy revellers canoodling while fireworks crackle at Valencia's Las Fallas festival. Even my accountant signs off her emails with " besos " (kisses).
After more than six years living in Spain, I've become used to these public displays of affection. But when a friend returned to Valencia after a trip to Japan, she noticed them immediately. Stepping out of the train station, she was greeted by a couple snogging on a bench. After her stint in a country where PDA is far less frequent, the sight filled her with relief. "I'm home," she thought.
It made me wonder: is Spain really a country of kissing? And what can these public displays of affection tell us about its culture, history and attitudes towards intimacy?
One explanation may lie in the way Spaniards use public spaces. In many parts of the country, everyday life takes place outdoors, in busy streets, cafes and parks.
A University of Warwick study found that Spain was among the countries that required the least personal space when meeting a new acquaintance – even less than its southern Mediterranean cousins Greece, Italy and Portugal. It's a tendency that plays out in Spain's bustling plazas, where terraces are filled with friends gathered shoulder-to-shoulder, sipping cañas (beers) in the sunshine.
Amparo Lasén, professor of sociology at Complutense University of Madrid , says that people in Spain tend to be more physically demonstrative than northern Europeans. "You notice more difference if you compare with Nordic countries or with England," she said.
Perhaps it's not that Spaniards are more affectionate than people elsewhere, but that they're more comfortable showing it. Kissing in public isn't necessarily a grand romantic gesture; it's simply an accepted part of everyday life.
Living arrangements may also play a part. Around 65% of Spain's population lives in flats – the highest proportion in the EU – while soaring property prices have made it increasingly difficult for young adults to move out of the family home.
Lasén suggests that limited privacy at home can push intimate moments into public spaces. "In Spain we have this housing crisis, meaning that we are more used to meeting our friends outside – going to bars, going to restaurants – rather than doing it at our homes," she says, adding that couples now have to seek out a secluded bench for some alone time – or nearly alone, at least.
But the housing crisis isn't the underlying reason for its public displays of affection, says Lasén. More important is the country's relaxed attitude towards them. "If no one gives you a bad look or just you don't care, well, that's the thing that makes it easier to have this kind of demonstration in public."
Isabel Nieto Tous, 28, who moved back in with her parents three years ago after living abroad, knows how awkward dating without much privacy can be. "I didn't want to tell my parents I was staying at people's houses, because it was a bit awkward, so I would say I was staying at a friend's place," she said.
Tous, who has lived in Japan, France, Germany and Tunisia, believes that dating is different in Spain; she says there's an instant warmth from the start. "People get very touchy and close very fast. Maybe you're in a situationship; you've met someone two times, and already you're holding hands in public and very touchy," she says.
"I think kissing in public is very accepted in general," she adds. "There's no differentiation between indoors and outdoors. People behave the same way in the intimate space as they do in the outside space."
While PDA may be a familiar sight in Spain today, expressions of sexuality were once tightly controlled. Under Francisco Franco’s dictatorship (1939-1975), conservative Catholic values and restrictive legislation dictated public behaviour, criminalising homosexuality and policing public displays of affection. Couples could even be fined for kissing in public.
After Franco's death in 1975, Spain underwent a profound cultural transformation. In Madrid, the exuberant counterculture movement known as La Movida Madrileña celebrated freedom and self-expression, with film-makers such as Pedro Almodóvar challenging the conservative values of the past. As the movement flourished, affection and sexuality became increasingly visible in public life.
But the sea-change didn't happen spontaneously. LGBT activists had been protesting for decades, clearing the path for a more open and accepting society. One pivotal protest took place in Madrid on 23 February 1987. The previous year, two women had been arrested for kissing in Madrid's Puerta del Sol and held in police custody for two days under the Escándalo Público (Public Scandal) law.
• What a German expert wants you to know about buying drinks in Germany
• Why is there no word for please in the Nordic languages?
• Why Swedes hate standing out
Their detention promoted local campaign groups to organise a mass kiss-in to draw attention to the case. From that year until around the 1990s, every Pride March in Madrid finished with a kiss in Puerta del Sol. Kissing in the street had become a powerful act of peaceful protest, and the public-scandal offence was abolished in 1988.
Today, public displays of affection can be seen across Spain, but that freedom isn't experienced equally. An older couple kissing on a public bench may attract more attention, while same-sex couples can face greater scrutiny, Lasén said. "Not everyone is equally comfortable showing their relationship."
For Paula Furió, a former wedding photographer in Valencia, kissing is a symbol of something much bigger. "There's still work to do, but Spanish society in general is very open. Kissing is like the tip of the iceberg: it gives you a sense of the freedom you can have in Spain. It's an expression of freedom."
It made me think back to my friend returning from Japan and the relief she felt at seeing a couple kissing on the bench. Perhaps she wasn't just happy to be home, she was happy to be in a country where authenticity overrules good manners. Maybe the most remarkable thing about kissing in Spain is how unremarkable it's become.

articles.title_orig: Making a $300 PS5 Instead of a $1,200 PS6 Would Be 'True Innovation', Says Ex-PlayStation Boss
articles.title_zh: Making a $300 PS5 Instead of a $1,200 PS6 Would Be 'True Innovation', Says Ex-PlayStation Boss
articles.content_orig:
As the PS5 generation approaches its sixth year, talk of what comes next has been circulating for a while, and with hardware as pricey as it is, the prospect of a PS6 isn't as exciting as it perhaps should be.
Opinion differs on that, of course, but it's generally accepted that Sony's next-gen machine is going to be eye-wateringly expensive , and it's currently anyone's guess as to whether it'll be worth a purchase.
Shawn Layden, formerly CEO of PlayStation and head of PlayStation Studios, has weighed in on the matter of next generation console hardware in a new interview.
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
Speaking on the Trophy Room podcast , he says Sony's best move wouldn't be to create a pricey, brand new console, it would be to revise the current hardware in order to sell it cheaper.
"The typical runway for platforms [is] six to eight years, you get a new one," Layden says. "But typically, that new one brought you something mind-blowing."
He speaks about the various innovative leaps from one console to the next, concluding that the move from PS4 to PS5 was mostly led by raytracing and teraflops. He expects technical aspects like this will be used to sell PS6 as well, but says these are "differences only dogs can hear", implying diminishing returns.
"We have enough power in the machine. The innovation needs to come not from making PS6 for $1200, it's to make another PS5 for $300. Now that would be true innovation."
As Layden points out, the current generation is the first to go up in price rather than down, and he thinks continuing with a PS6 at such a premium price point, and focusing on incremental increases in power, risks alienating the audience.
"What the company needs to do is do what it's never done, which is, don't iterate the console," he says. "Make it smaller, make it cheaper, do all the things you can around that. The silicon is fine, the OS is fine. It's more than enough power to build the kind of games all of us want to play."
While his words of wisdom may ring true for many, Sony itself is forging ahead with its next-gen plans , so we'll likely be faced with a costly new console within the next couple of years.

articles.title_orig: Man jailed over racist Badenoch death threats
articles.title_zh: Man jailed over racist Badenoch death threats
articles.content_orig:
A man has been jailed for sending the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch emails threatening to shoot her dead.
Ex-teacher Kieran Kyle sent three emails on 2 May to the Tory party leader in which he made racist references and claimed to have been in the IRA, the court heard.
The 43-year-old, from Gillingham in Kent, pleaded guilty on 22 September at Westminster Magistrates' Court to two counts of sending communications of an indecent or offensive nature.
Kyle was sentenced to 20 weeks in prison at the same court on Monday.
In a victim impact statement read to the court, Badenoch and her husband Hamish said the "malicious communications and targeted harassment" not only had an effect on them, but also undermined "a healthy democracy".
In two of the emails, Kyle had made racist references and written: "I'm ex-IRA, so Bloody Sunday references from you are going to give you trouble," the court heard.
The messages were sent on the day Badenoch apologised for footage from Bloody Sunday being mistakenly used in a social media clip to criticise a parliamentary Bill on legacy issues in Northern Ireland.
The Tory leader had said she did not sign off the video and that it was sent out by "very young people".
The video criticising the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, posted to her social media channels on 28 April, showed Badenoch saying the Labour legislation would "drag" Troubles veterans back to court.
Thirteen unarmed civilians were shot dead when members of the Army's Parachute Regiment opened fire on civil rights demonstrators in the Bogside area of Londonderry on 30 January 1972, a date that became known as Bloody Sunday.
The court heard Kyle had also sent an email to Badenoch's husband Hamish on 29 April, which used a racist term and said she had a "big mouth" and he should "put a leash on her".
Prosecutor Ben Holt said the North West Essex MP and her husband were left "distressed" and "upset", particularly by the "racist language and threats of violence used towards them".
He added Cheryl Bacon, head of Badenoch's parliamentary office, said the emails were "disgusting" and "distressing" to read.
Baiju Thittala, defending, told the court Kyle "did not know" who Badenoch was at the time of the offences, adding "he only realised later, once he had sent the emails".
Asked by the judge how Kyle, a former secondary school teacher, could not know who Badenoch was, Thittala said: "He just 'Googled' it and it came up as the opposition leader."
The judge said: "The first emails were sent to Mr Badenoch, so I don't think he did not appreciate who Mrs Badenoch was.
"So he clearly knew who Mrs Badenoch was because he researched her husband's details first."
The Badenochs said in their victim impact statement: "Our primary concern arising from this offence is not the personal impact on us, but the wider consequences that malicious communications and targeted harassment have on our democratic life.
"When individuals choose to intimidate, threaten, or aggressively target elected representatives or public figures, the harm extends far beyond any single person. It undermines a healthy democracy."
The continued: "Public service relies on people being willing to step forward, often at significant personal cost, to represent their communities and contribute to public life.
"Increasingly, however, those who do so face hostility, harassment, and attempts to silence or intimidate them."
The judge also handed Kyle a restraining order, meaning he cannot contact Badenoch, her husband or her parliamentary office for five years.

articles.title_orig: Quest Diagnostics pays $13M to settle kickback allegations involving NY Giants tickets
articles.title_zh: Quest Diagnostics pays $13M to settle kickback allegations involving NY Giants tickets
articles.content_orig:
Make your contribution now and help Gothamist thrive in 2026. Donate today
Gothamist is funded by sponsors and member donations
Quest Diagnostics paid over $13 million to resolve allegations that it provided health care providers and executives illegal kickbacks in the form of New York Giants tickets and access to exclusive events, according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office of New Jersey.
U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer on Friday said the clinical lab operator, based in Secaucus, NJ, offered clients Giants suite seats and access to training camp in exchange for business referrals.
Frazer said Quest violated the Anti-Kickback Statute, which prohibits offering, soliciting, or taking payment to encourage the use of services or items covered by Medicare, Medicaid and other federally funded healthcare programs.
“Kickbacks to referring providers, especially by lab companies, corrupt medical judgment, lead to unnecessary lab testing, cause providers to steer patients to labs that offer inducements, and squander taxpayer money,” Frazer said in a statement.
The settlement resolves allegations that, between July 25, 2013 and Aug. 3, 2022, Quest violated the kickback statute and that the firm submitted false claims for lab services that Medicare and New York and New Jersey Medicaid paid for, officials said.
In 2013, Quest entered into a naming rights and sponsorship agreement with the New York Giants. As part of this agreement, the Giants provided suites to Quest for home games at MetLife Stadium. The firm also gained various marketing, commercial programming and hospitality benefits, according to prosecutors.
Quest then provided clients access to Giants home game suite seats, VIP training camp, draft “chalk-talk” presentations, and NFL scouting events for free, according to officials.
After inviting clients to the games and events, Quest calculated the revenue it received from them for up to one year after entertaining them, officials said. In addition, the company then billed Medicare, as well as New York and New Jersey Medicaid for claims for lab testing that were referred from the clients that they entertained, prosecutors said.
The New York Giants organization, which is based in New Jersey, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Under the settlement Quest is also required to enter into a five-year corporate integrity agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services-Office of Inspector General, requiring the firm to obtain an independent review organization to audit the company.
A spokesperson for Quest said the firm denies any allegations of wrongdoing or violation of the law, but agreed to the settlement to “put the matter behind us.”
“We adhere to a policy of strict compliance with the laws and regulations governing our business,” spokesperson Amanda Rivera said in a statement. “Since last year, we have shared information about this settlement, which includes a Corporate Integrity Agreement, with the public through our regulatory filings. In many respects, the CIA mirrors our existing rigorous compliance program, and we have been complying with its requirements.”

articles.title_orig: Russia-Ukraine war: Nine foreigners caught trying to leave South Africa to join conflict
articles.title_zh: Russia-Ukraine war: Nine foreigners caught trying to leave South Africa to join conflict
articles.content_orig:
Nine foreigners have been arrested in South Africa after they were caught allegedly trying to leave the country to fight in the war between Russia and the Ukraine, police say.
The group, aged between 20 and 26, were arrested in and around Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team on Sunday evening.
They were caught as they were "preparing to board flights out of the country", authorities added, but their final destination is unclear.
The group is accused of contravening South Africa's laws, which outlaw mercenary activity without government permission.
Police said the group were arrested at South Africa's biggest airport, OR Tambo, and a hotel in Bruma, east of Johannesburg by a multidisciplinary team that involved Interpol.
The police statement added that the involvement of Interpol and other international law enforcement agencies indicated that the suspects had also allegedly violated laws in their respective home countries, prompting cooperation with South African authorities.
Authorities declined to disclose the group's nationalities but confirmed that none of them resided in South Africa.
They have also not said whether the group allegedly intended to fight for Russia or Ukraine nor provided details of the organisations allegedly involved in facilitating their travel.
Citizens of several African countries, including Kenya, Ghana and South Africa, have gone to fight for Russia in Ukraine - some they had been duped and had not realised where they were going.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment estimated earlier this year that more than 1,700 people from 36 countries in Africa have been recruited to fight for Russia.
Kenya at the time estimated that 252 citizens had been illegally conscripted in Russia. In March, Foreign Minister Musalia Mudavadi visited Moscow to address the issue.
He said at the time that an agreement had been reached to stop recruiting Kenyan nationals.
In February, Ghana said that 55 of its citizens had been killed in the conflict, with 272 believed to have been lured to fight since the war started in 2022.
The same month, South Africa secured the return of 17 South Africans who were allegedly tricked into joining the war.
In December last year, South African authorities arrested five people, including a journalist, for allegedly recruiting people to join the war.
Ukraine has also been recruiting foreign nationals, including from Africa.
The nine arrested are expected to appear in court either later on Monday or Tuesday.
